title: The association between the acute:chronic workload ratio and running-related injuries in Dutch runners: a prospective cohort study
authors: Nakaoka G, Barboza SD, Verhagen E, van Mechelen W, Hespanhol L
population: 435 runners; secondary analysis of three studies with the same running-related injury (RRI) surveillance system; biweekly exposure and RRI over 18-65 weeks; ACWR = last 2 weeks over the mean of the last 4-12 weeks, by uncoupled, coupled and EWMA methods
findings: Runners with ACWR under 0.70 had about 10% predicted probability of RRI (9.6%; 95% CrI 7.5-12.4) versus about 1% (1.3%; 95% CrI 0.7-1.7) for ACWR above 1.38.
The association was significant, small to moderate (1-10%), and inverse: the higher the ACWR, the lower the RRI risk, following a smooth L-shaped second-order polynomial decay curve.
Hours or kilometres gave similar results; coupled and uncoupled methods were similar and the uncoupled method best discriminated strata.
The EWMA method yielded sparse and non-significant results.
limitations: Secondary analysis of three cohorts; association not causation; a low ACWR may reflect detraining or return from rest, which the abstract does not test. Self-report and population type (recreational) are not stated in the abstract.
implications: For runners, do not impose spike-based ACWR limits; this study shows no increase in injury risk with high ACWR and more injury at low ACWR.
Use an ACWR-like value at most as a descriptive detraining or return-from-break flag (below about 0.7 in this study), not as a prescriptive cap.

verification.notes: Crossref confirms title, Sports Med, 2021-05-30. Numbers match Europe PMC abstract. Removed 'self-reported' and 'recreational' as abstract-unsupported wording.
